subsection: 5. Best practice for the use of supplements

notes.b: Athletes are often tempted to look for an extra edge beyond ordinary meals. A dietary supplement is the kind of product they turn to, and it carries a risk that ordinary food does not.
points: A dietary supplement is a product taken in addition to the normal diet, such as a powder, tablet, drink or gel.
It supplies nutrients or other substances intended to improve health or performance, so it is meant to add to meals, not replace them.
Supplements are not regulated like medicines, so a product can contain substances that are not on its label. This is why athletes cannot simply trust what a tub says.
notes.tip: Do not present supplements as necessary or risk-free. Give the benefit and the risk together.

notes.b: The danger of an unregulated product is not just poor quality. For an athlete who is drug-tested, it can lead to a ban even if they never meant to cheat.
points: Some supplements are contaminated with prohibited substances (banned drugs picked up during manufacture), or contain undeclared ones that are missing from the label.
Under strict liability the athlete is responsible for a positive test, whatever the source of the substance. Blaming the supplement or the manufacturer is not a defence.
Taking a supplement without intending to cheat can still produce an anti-doping violation; this is inadvertent doping (doping by accident).
notes.tip: To explain why supplement use can lead to an anti-doping violation, link the three ideas: not regulated like medicines, possible contamination or undeclared substances, and strict liability.

notes.h: Best practice before using a supplement
notes.b: Because of these risks, athletes should work through three questions before taking anything: can food do the job, is there a real need, and does the evidence support it?
points: Food first: meet nutritional needs through a balanced diet before considering supplements, because a supplement is an addition to food, not a substitute for it.
Needs assessment: a qualified professional, such as a sports dietitian or doctor, decides whether there is a genuine need and whether the supplement will help this athlete.
Evidence: use only supplements with good scientific evidence for the athlete's activity, so that the benefit is proven for that sport and not just claimed.
notes.tip: Do not present supplements as necessary. Food first and a professional needs assessment come before any supplement.

notes.b: Once an athlete and a professional decide a supplement is justified, the next job is to lower the chance that it contains a banned substance.
points: Choose batch-tested products (each production batch checked for banned substances) from third-party testing programmes, which are run independently of the manufacturer; this reduces the risk but does not remove it.
Check every ingredient against the Prohibited List, the official list of substances and methods banned in sport.
Keep the packaging, batch number and receipt, so the product can be traced if a problem arises.
Never buy from unknown online sources, because there is no assurance about what the product contains.
notes.tip: When asked for best practice, give the specific steps: batch-tested, third-party programmes, ingredient check, keep packaging, batch number and receipt, and no unknown online sources.

notes.b: Even a safe, tested product can cause problems if it is used badly, so how and when it is taken matters as well as what it is.
points: Use the correct dose and timing, because more is not better and a supplement works best when taken at the right moment.
Trial the supplement in training, never for the first time in competition, so that any bad reaction happens when the result does not count.
Monitor side effects (unwanted effects such as stomach upset) and stop if they appear.
Young athletes: supplements are generally not recommended for under-18s, so diet should come first.
notes.tip: Outline challenges of taking supplements using real points: side effects, cost, unnecessary if the diet is adequate, and the doping risk.

notes.b: Protein is the supplement most associated with building muscle. It comes as powders and bars that are quick to use.
points: Function: muscle repair and growth after resistance (strength) or high-volume (large amounts of) training.
Suits: athletes who do heavy resistance or high-volume training.
Challenge: it is convenient, but often unnecessary when the diet already supplies enough protein.
notes.tip: Some questions ask for food supplements other than protein, so be ready with others and their reasons.

notes.b: Creatine works on the energy supply of muscle for very short, powerful efforts, so it suits sports built from repeated bursts.
points: Function: raises muscle phosphocreatine stores (phosphocreatine is a fuel store in muscle used for quick energy), improving repeated short maximal efforts and recovery between them.
Suits: sprinting, team games and weightlifting, because each involves short all-out efforts.
Challenge: weight gain from water retention.
Not prohibited: creatine is not a prohibited substance.
notes.tip: Exam questions may exclude creatine, for example by saying you may not use it. Know at least three other supplements, each with its function and effect.

notes.b: Caffeine is a familiar substance that also has effects useful to athletes. Its status in anti-doping rules is worth knowing precisely.
points: Function: a stimulant (a substance that raises alertness and activity in the nervous system) that can reduce perceived effort (how hard exercise feels) and improve alertness and endurance.
Suits: endurance events and games that need sustained alertness.
Challenge: side effects include anxiety, poor sleep and stomach upset.
Not prohibited: caffeine is on WADA's monitoring programme, not the Prohibited List. WADA is the World Anti-Doping Agency, and monitored means it is watched, not banned.
notes.tip: Name a supplement and justify why athletes use it. For caffeine, give the function and the effect on performance, and say it is permitted but monitored.

notes.b: In long events the body loses fluid and runs low on fuel. Sports drinks and gels replace both while the athlete is still competing.
points: Function: they supply fluid, electrolytes (salts such as sodium lost in sweat) and carbohydrate (the body's main fuel) during long events.
Suits: long endurance events.
Challenge: sugar, calories and cost, and unnecessary for short or low-intensity activity, where water and a normal diet are enough.
notes.tip: Give function and effect on performance: fluid, electrolytes and carbohydrate during long events.

notes.b: Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts, and normally a balanced diet provides them. A supplement has a narrow use here.
points: Function: to correct a diagnosed deficiency (a shortage confirmed by a professional), such as iron or vitamin D.
Use: only to correct a diagnosed deficiency, not as a routine addition to the diet, so a healthy athlete with a balanced diet does not need them.
notes.tip: Do not list steroids or EPO as supplements. Those are prohibited drugs and belong under drugs and sport.

notes.h: Investigating a supplement for one activity
notes.b: The syllabus asks you to investigate supplement use in one activity you have chosen. The answer is built from the activity's demands, matched to the supplements that suit them.
points: Structure: describe the activity's demands, including its duration, intensity and main energy systems (the body's ways of releasing energy for movement).
Structure: list the supplements used in the activity, with their claimed benefits, the evidence, the risks and the best-practice guidance.
Structure: end with a conclusion on whether and how a performer should use them.
Worked example, Gaelic football: a match is a long game of repeated sprints, changes of pace and physical contact.
Link: the repeated sprints match creatine, whose benefit lies in repeated short maximal efforts.
Link: the length of a match makes sports drinks useful for fluid and carbohydrate.
Link: recovery after heavy training is where protein has its role.

Conclusion: a player could use creatine for repeated sprints, protein for recovery and sports drinks in matches, but only after food-first habits are in place, a qualified professional has confirmed the need, and batch-tested products are chosen.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to investigate the uses of a supplement in one selected activity. Tie each supplement to a demand of that activity and finish with a conclusion.

keyTerms.definition: A product taken in addition to the normal diet to supply nutrients or other substances intended to improve health or performance.
An anti-doping violation caused by taking a substance without intending to cheat, such as a contaminated supplement.
The presence of a prohibited substance in a product when it is not listed on the label.
Testing a sample from a production batch of a product to check its contents.
Independent testing of a product by an organisation other than its manufacturer.
The principle of meeting nutritional needs through a balanced diet before using supplements.
A qualified professional who advises athletes on nutrition.
A substance that raises muscle phosphocreatine stores, improving repeated short maximal efforts.
A high-energy compound stored in muscle that supplies energy for short maximal efforts.
A stimulant that can reduce perceived effort and improve alertness and endurance.
A powder or bar that adds protein to the diet to support muscle repair and growth.

questions.prompt: Identify three sports supplements, their function and the performance effect of each. You may not use creatine.
questions.model: 1. Protein powder: its function is muscle repair and growth after training, so its performance effect is better recovery between sessions and muscle growth over time. 2. Caffeine: a stimulant whose function is to increase alertness; its performance effect is that it can reduce perceived effort and improve endurance. 3. Energy gel: its function is to supply carbohydrate during long events, so its performance effect is that it sustains energy for the performer when a long event is under way.

questions.prompt: Discuss best practice for an athlete considering the use of dietary supplements.
questions.model: First, food first: the athlete should meet nutritional needs through a balanced diet, because most supplements are unnecessary when the diet is adequate. Second, a qualified professional such as a sports dietitian or doctor should assess whether there is a genuine need and whether the supplement will help this athlete. Third, the athlete should use only products with good scientific evidence for their activity. Fourth, choose batch-tested products from third-party testing programmes, check every ingredient against the Prohibited List, and keep the packaging, batch number and receipt; never buy from unknown online sources, since contamination can cause a positive test. Fifth, trial the supplement in training, use the correct dose and timing, monitor side effects, and never try it for the first time in competition. Young athletes under 18 should generally focus on diet rather than supplements.

questions.prompt: Name a sports supplement and give two reasons an athlete might use it.
questions.model: Protein powder. First, it supplies protein for muscle repair after resistance or high-volume training. Second, it is a convenient source of protein when a proper meal is not available soon after training.
